items.definition: Wind generation output depends heavily on the exact physical location of a turbine, not just the general region — nearby sites can have very different wind resource quality.
items.core_idea: Terrain features (e.g., a hilltop versus the sheltered side of the same hill) can produce sharply different wind speeds at locations only a short distance apart, so wind resource assessment must be done at the individual turbine/site level rather than assumed uniform across a project area.
key_points: Two nearby locations can have materially different wind conditions due to terrain (e.g., hilltop vs. hillside shelter).
This makes wind output forecasting and siting more granular/site-specific than for some other generation types.
relationships: Affects capacity factor estimates used in wind project economics
trading_implications: Forecast error for a specific wind farm can't be assumed to track a regional average; site-level historical output data is more reliable than nearby-site proxies.
common_misunderstandings: Assuming that wind conditions are roughly uniform across a small geographic area.

items.topic: Wake effect and wind farm layout
items.definition: When one turbine sits downwind of another, it receives turbulent, disrupted airflow rather than clean wind, which lowers its output and increases mechanical stress.
items.core_idea: The upwind turbine disturbs the wind flow reaching downwind turbines, so wind farm layouts are typically arranged in lines or otherwise spaced out to minimize this interference between units.
key_points: A downwind turbine experiences chaotic/disrupted airflow caused by the turbine upwind of it.
Wind farms are commonly organized in lines or spread out specifically to reduce this inter-turbine disruption.
relationships: Related to overall wind farm capacity factor and turbine spacing decisions
trading_implications: Physical layout constraints limit how densely a wind farm can be built on a given parcel, which caps nameplate capacity per unit of land.

items.topic: Public opposition to wind power: bird mortality and aesthetics
items.definition: The two most common sources of consumer/community opposition to wind farms are harm to migratory birds and objections to the visual appearance of turbines.
items.core_idea: Turbines are often sited on migratory bird corridors because those corridors have the steady winds turbines need, which puts them at risk of collision with spinning blades; separately, some communities object to wind farms simply because they consider them visually unappealing.
key_points: Steady, sustained winds along bird migration corridors make those corridors attractive turbine sites, creating overlap with bird flight paths.
Birds can be struck and killed by turbine blades in these areas.
Environmental groups worry that widespread wind adoption could significantly harm wild bird populations.
Aesthetic objections (turbines viewed as unattractive) are a separate, non-environmental driver of local opposition.
trading_implications: Community and environmental opposition is a project development/siting risk that can delay or block new wind capacity, which is relevant context when assessing future wind supply growth.

items.topic: Transmission overload risk from correlated wind ramp-up
items.definition: Wind power is often constrained by limited long-distance transmission capacity, and because turbines in a region tend to start producing together when wind picks up, the shared transmission lines can become congested/overloaded.
items.core_idea: Remote wind farms depend on costly long-distance transmission lines to reach load; because wind across a region tends to rise simultaneously, all turbines can ramp up output together and overload that shared transmission path, similar to a rush-hour traffic jam limiting how much generation can actually reach consumers.
key_points: Long-distance transmission to remote wind sites is expensive to build and maintain.
Wind output across a region tends to rise together, so many turbines can start producing at the same time.
This simultaneous ramp-up can overload the transmission lines carrying that power to load, creating congestion analogous to rush-hour traffic.
trading_implications: Correlated regional wind ramps can drive transmission congestion, which is a relevant driver of locational basis and congestion cost between a wind-heavy zone and load centers.
Curtailment risk during high-wind periods should be considered when evaluating expected wind output that actually reaches the grid.
common_misunderstandings: Assuming turbine-level output alone determines delivered power, without accounting for transmission capacity limits.

items.topic: Fast-start backup generation needed for wind ramp-down
items.definition: Because regional wind output can also drop off simultaneously across many turbines, the grid needs backup generation capable of starting and stopping very quickly to replace that lost output.
items.core_idea: When wind stops blowing across a region, many turbines can stop producing at once, forcing the grid to bring fast-start backup generation on- and off-line quickly; balancing is harder if that backup generation isn't located near the wind farms, since wind units themselves are typically sited in remote areas while fast-start units usually are not.
key_points: Wind output can fall off simultaneously across many turbines in a region when wind conditions change.
This requires backup (fast-start) generation to rapidly come on- and off-line to offset the loss.
Fast-start generators are typically not located in the same remote areas as wind farms, which complicates balancing power flows across the grid.
relationships: Transmission overload risk from correlated wind ramp-up
trading_implications: Wind's simultaneous ramp-down risk supports the case for flexible, quick-response capacity (e.g., fast-start gas peakers or battery storage) sited to help balance the grid when wind output drops.
related_topics: Transmission overload risk from correlated wind ramp-up
